items.title: /healthz no longer touches Postgres, so a replica with a permanently broken database stays Ready
items.notes: The probe was changed to return 204 with no database check, as the task asks. A replica whose database is permanently unreachable (bad credentials after a rotation, a wrong host) stays in service, and every request on it then waits in db.Retry with no upper bound except the client giving up. A cap on the wait, or a separate readiness signal such as 'away longer than N minutes', would be cheap. Promoted to JS-056.

items.title: A staged segment file is no longer removed when the final UPDATE fails for a non-outage reason
items.notes: In Worker.upload, os.Remove(name) moved after the UPDATE and only the IsAway error returns before it. A non-away error now leaves the file on disk until the job's working directory is cleaned up. Alternative: remove the file only on success or on errWaiting.

items.notes: IsAway returns true for any net.Error, including S3 or segment-store timeouts. worker.run now adds `|| db.IsAway(err)` to the cancelled branch, so a store outage that returns a net error ends the job as `cancelled`. Such jobs are never refused, and viewers restart them without limit instead of seeing the last-attempt-failed protection. The same IsAway test would also start an outage tracker and pr

items.notes: /healthz now always answers 204. Alternative: fail /healthz only once db.Of(pool).Total() for the current outage exceeds a bound well above a switchover, such as 2 minutes. items.title: Process-global sync.Map keyed by pool, and a tracker that learns only from failures
items.notes: db.Of(pool) looks the tracker up in a package-level sync.Map that Open fills and nothing removes. Every caller that was handed some other pool (tests, tools) silently gets a nil tracker that never says 'away'. Holding the tracker on a small wrapper type or in Server/Jobs/Worker fields would cost a few constructor changes and would make the missing-tracker case a compile error, not a silent no-op.

items.title: Worker logs an ERROR for a Postgres switchover it survives
items.notes: Any Postgres switchover or restart ends the worker's liveness connection. The worker logs at Error level 'the worker's liveness connection ended; its jobs go on, and it claims none until it holds the lock again and its row is there' (line 285), then at Info 'holds its liveness lock again ... its jobs went on'. Operators see ERROR lines for an event the build survives. Reading only.

items.notes: fail() now returns without any log whenever r.Context().Err() != nil, for every error and not only outage errors. Operators lose the diagnostic for real failures on abandoned requests. Reading only.

items.title: e2e recorder drops every non-JSON response, so 'no JSON body where the schema gives one' cannot fire in e2e
items.notes: The recorder returns early unless content-type matches /json/. If a route the schema types as JSON answers 200 with text/html (such as an SPA fallback) or an empty body with another content type, jellyfin-web receives it, nothing is recorded, and the gate passes. The differential tier does pass the content type, so only e2e has the hole. Reading evidence only: the filter sits at conform.mjs:14.

items.title: Sweep sends every listed request, startup included, with the signed-in token, and ignores each row's auth field
items.notes: Startup requests (/System/Info/Public, /Users/Public, /QuickConnect/Enabled) are sent by clients before sign-in with no Token. The sweep always sends the user's token and never reads the row's `auth` field, so a regression that makes those routes require auth passes. This is the criterion's 'Authorization header form' item: it is listed but never sent.

items.title: A listed request that answers non-2xx is excused when Jellyfin gives the same status
items.notes: The criterion says each listed request must answer 2xx and never 404. sweep() skips a failure when `reference.answers(r, status)` returns true, meaning Jellyfin answered the same status. A route that 404s on both servers (for example because of a fixture id mismatch) is excused, and the schema check never sees its answer. Closed by the product owner: duplicate of BL-072.

items.title: Fence can answer ok for a job the keeper has just cut
items.notes: The keeper cuts a job (timer giveUp sets over) while a renewal sent before the cut is in flight. The renewal then finds the row ours, and attempt() answers pending asks with until=sent+lease, even though the job is over. The put checks only the clock, so a put can start after the job was cut. It is bounded by one round trip, and the work context is cancelled, so the put probably fails. Not reproduced.

items.title: The keeper's two tables are renewed one after the other on one goroutine
items.notes: A transcode renewal that blocks on a row lock or a slow answer takes up to bound (half a heartbeat) before the subtitle table is tried, and the keeper's connect can take up to lease/2 before either table is tried. The cut timers are independent, so the lease stays safe. The cost is less margin for the subtitle table, and a slow connect delays a fence answer for up to half a lease. Alternative: connect in a separate goroutine, or renew the tables concurrently on two connections. That adds a third connection per worker and conflicts with the 'two connections' design.

items.title: Per-job lost reason is queried on the keeper's connection inside the single loop
items.notes: When several jobs are found lost in one renewal, attempt() calls j.lost for each in turn, each bounded by half a heartbeat on the keeper's connection. With k lost jobs and a slow database, the keeper's next renewal for the other jobs is delayed by up to k half-heartbeats. The cut timers still protect the lease. Alternative: fetch the reasons in one query or afterwards, off the renewal path.

items.title: Abandoned Put goroutine can leak and may still write the segment later
items.notes: A store Put that ignores its context and never returns: worker.put returns on ctx.Done but the goroutine and the open file handle stay until the Put returns, which may be never. A Posix-like store whose Put ignores ctx can also finish later and rename the segment into place after the job was cancelled (written by a non-owner; no DB record, so harmless to correctness but visible in the store).

items.title: Per-put fence adds one keeper renewal round trip per put
items.notes: upload() used to fence once per upload and now fences before each put (init, then segment). Each fence asks the keeper to renew the job's lease, so a segment upload makes two renewal round trips where it made one. Doing the fence once per upload and checking it against a fresh clock before each put would not do: a put can now outlast a lease, so the second put needs a fresh fence. The cost is small and the choice is sound.

items.title: Snapshot safety rests on panic/recover and on every refusal calling refuse/notFound/waitForPostgres
items.notes: A later handler edit that writes an error with plain http.Error or http.NotFound on a stream route would, when run from the snapshot during an outage, answer the viewer from the snapshot instead of waiting for Postgres. The old design had the same risk the other way round: an offline handler had to opt in to each answer. The new default is the safer one, but the guard is a convention with no mechanical check. internal/api/snapshot.go lines 70-100: waitForPostgres panics with errWait and serveFromSnapshot recovers it. Direct http.Error calls remain reachable in shared handlers, for example in serveSource. The new internal/api/oneroute_test.go checks each row, but nothing fails a new http.Error call placed before a snapshot-aware refusal. A cheap alternative is a lint or grep test that bans http.Error and http.NotFound in the stream-role handler files.

items.title: Partial push of a version leaves it unrepairable

If a later push fails (network, quota), a rerun finds X.Y.Z already exists and fails by design, so the release can never get its -fixtures tag; the only way out is a new version. Pushing the -fixtures tag and the main tags before the bare version tag would shorten the window.

items.title: Concurrency group per sha lets a pending run be replaced

Promote if it fails on the merge queue, a third time locally, or if jellyscale itself (not the test stack) is shown to have used up the connections (then with JS-092). D-042: if the e2e scenario that failed the merge queue on 2026-11-20 is one of these three, the promote rule is met; it is then JS-155's seventh sighting and this item becomes promoted. If it is another scenario, this item is unchanged.

items.title: An operator who declares proxies while every client still arrives from one upstream address gets all viewers refused together
items.notes: Every viewer shares the counted address, so they are refused together. The server could notice many devices and names behind one counted address and warn, or keep a known device out of the address refusal. Beside BL-210; needs its own brief. Promote when an operator reports viewers refused together, or with JS-056 if its ingress is shown to pass one address for all clients.

items.title: The memory of unknown sign-in names forgets more than its bound needs under parallel floods, and never ages
items.notes: Two sightings. Round 3 (command): bound 200, 24 workers, 4,800 names left 153 rows; the striped counter is summed without a lock. Round 4 (reading only): signin_unknown keeps up to 100,000 rows of invented names for good, counters included, after their failures have aged out; a later flood evicts by fewest failures, then oldest, so stale high-count names outlive fresh ones. The stated bound holds and no viewer is refused by it; an operator sees a small table that fills and stays full. Promote when someone shows, at the shipped bound, a real name told from an invented one with fewer requests than the documented bound implies, or a stale row changing who is refused.

items.title: A right password whose sign-in ends after the match began leaves a counted failure
items.notes: Two sightings, both reading only. The failure is stored before the password is compared and taken back after. Round 3: the take-back runs on the request context, so a client hang-up could leave the count. Round 4: the take-back detaches its context but runs only when the handler reaches it, so a client disconnect, a dead process or a timed-out comparison leaves it. Which of these holds is unverified. What a viewer would notice: at 19 failures the name is refused to new devices for 15 minutes with no wrong password given. Promote at once if a test shows a client hang-up alone, database healthy, leaves a count, or a viewer is refused after right passwords only.

items.title: A forwarded entry with a port or brackets is accepted as its address
items.notes: Promote when a named ingress is shown to write entries that way.

items.title: A filtered e2e run (E2E_ONLY) of the refused-sign-in scenario fails the cors gate's 'checked no JSON responses' summary
items.notes: Beside BL-075. Cause, from round 4 (reading only): responses are recorded for the gate's main page alone, and the scenario opens a page of its own, so the JSON jellyfin-web gets during a refused sign-in is neither written nor held to the schema; run alone, the gate has checked nothing and the run-level check fails. No viewer notices; the refusal's answer as jellyfin-web receives it is not held to Jellyfin's schema in e2e. Promote when a second task's filtered command fails the same way, or a refused sign-in's body is found to differ from the schema.

items.title: The compose stack as shipped cannot name a guessing client or bound per address
items.notes: Measure whether Docker keeps a remote client's source address on a port published to the network, and what publishing that way exposes. Promote when an operator runs the compose stack reachable from a network, or when the measurement is made.

items.title: A right password being checked counts as a failure meanwhile, so a second sign-in in that moment can be refused for 15 minutes' worth
items.notes: Reading only, not run. With a name at 19 failures (or 9 on a known device or from one address), a right password is held as the 20th for the 80 ms or so its comparison takes; another sign-in arriving then is answered 403 with Retry-After 900, though the refusal is gone once the first completes. A viewer notices only while their name is already one short of refusal, and a retry succeeds, but jellyfin-web tells them they are not authorized. Same cause as BL-215. Promote if a test shows two right passwords together, with no wrong one in between, getting a 403, or a viewer reports being refused with the right password.

items.title: The unknown-name flood check drives a function no sign-in calls
items.notes: Reading only. JS-145's criterion 6 says the flood drives the one function the handler calls to count a failed sign-in for a name; the check drives FailName and NameRefusal, which only tests call, while a sign-in goes through Begin (said to reach the same counting step, with the address and device steps before it). So the memory bound is shown on the counting step, not on a sign-in. Fix when a task next touches sign-in (JS-037 or JS-033): the flood goes through what a sign-in calls and the test-only pair goes. Promote sooner if the two paths are shown to count differently.

items.title: The procedure for confirming declared proxies has no branch for an ingress that sends no usable forwarded address
items.notes: Reading only. An operator declares trustedProxies for an ingress that writes no X-Forwarded-For and follows docs/running.md: 11 wrong sign-ins for an invented name. The doc promises ten 401s and then a refusal with a log line naming the address; they get eleven 401s and no refusal line, and the only hint is a warning written once per process, which the same paragraph's 'a single failed sign-in writes no log line' contradicts. They cannot tell a working bound from an absent one. With BL-210, BL-213, BL-216 and BL-218 this is one operator experience: declaring proxies and knowing it worked. Product owner: amend JS-056 with a criterion that the confirmation procedure, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted; mark this promoted once tasks/prd.json carries it. Promote ahead of JS-056 if an operator reports following the procedure and being unable to tell.

items.title: Apps ask for trickplay tiles and for sign-in by code, which are not built; what their viewers see is not known
items.notes: Roku, Streamyfin, Fladder and Jellyfin for Android request Trickplay routes and get 404 (read from source). Whether they show no preview or an error is unverified. /QuickConnect/Enabled answers false today (internal/api/system.go, read by the lead), so apps should not offer a code. JS-075 records both. Promote: if an app shows an error or offers a code that fails, plan the smallest answer that makes it quiet (an item that advertises no trickplay) ahead of JS-053 and JS-037; if apps are quiet, close.

items.title: The two saved Remember settings (audio, subtitle selections) may do nothing; a per-series memory across devices is beyond Jellyfin
items.notes: Issue #117. JS-041's capture records whether a progress report naming a subtitle track changes the next default with RememberSubtitleSelections on; nothing records the audio twin. Promote: if Jellyfin 12.4 carries a choice to the next episode and jellyscale does not, a saved setting does nothing (as BL-151, D-025): plan it after JS-041, with the audio twin observed the same way. A memory beyond what Jellyfin applies waits for data that viewers re-pick tracks episode after episode. Jellyfin 12.4 remembers a viewer's audio pick per film across reloads and sign-ins (compat/captures/audio-menu-12.4.md, 'On return'); jellyscale does not (JS-147, D-029). Audio half planned as JS-157 (D-039); this item stays open for memory beyond Jellyfin.

items.title: PlaybackInfo may ignore EnableDirectPlay, EnableDirectStream, AllowVideoStreamCopy and AllowAudioStreamCopy
items.notes: Issue #224; unverified at runtime. Evidence: (1) JS-075's records of each client's PlaybackInfo request: does any played app send one of these as false, and what did its viewer see; (2) the lead observes jellyfin-web 12.4 on a film the browser accepts but cannot play: what its second PlaybackInfo carries and what Jellyfin answers. If a supported client sends them and its viewer is left with a film that does not play, plan a task ahead of JS-054 (goal 1), with a brief on the CPU a client can then demand. If none sends them, close.

items.title: GET /Items may ignore nameLessThan and nameStartsWithOrGreater
items.notes: Issue #227. Evidence, by the lead: what jellyfin-web 12.4's letter picker sends for '#' and for a letter, and whether jellyscale's answer to those requests matches Jellyfin's in the differential tier. If jellyfin-web sends a parameter jellyscale ignores, add it to JS-068 (goal 3). A count-only jump for TV grids waits for a supported app recorded sending it (JS-075, JS-065).

items.title: Hard-of-hearing and audio-description tracks: flags on a film's own tracks, and whether a film can start in audio description
items.notes: Issue #114. External files already carry IsHearingImpaired (DOMAINS). Evidence, by the lead: (1) whether compat/differences.yaml lists IsHearingImpaired on a film's own subtitle tracks under JS-068; if so it is already planned there; (2) how many dogfood films carry an audio track marked for the visually impaired, and whether JS-121's rule makes any of them the default for a viewer's language. If one does, plan a task after JS-041 (goal 1: playback never surprises). If none, labelling waits for a supported app that shows it. Generated audio description is dropped as research-grade (D-036). A generated subtitle would lack sound cues, so it is not a hard-of-hearing track and must not be flagged as one (BL-232).

items.title: A film with no subtitle in the viewer's reading language has none to offer (generated or translated subtitles)
items.notes: AI research 2026-11-20 (D-036). Promote on data, in this order: (1) the share of dogfood films with no subtitle, inside or beside the file, in any account's SubtitleLanguagePreference, and the share with none at all; (2) the films' spoken languages (JS-117). If (1) is a share viewers meet weekly, plan a spike first, not a build: wall time, cores and memory per 2 h film on a dogfood worker's CPU and iGPU; invented lines over music and silence against films with human subtitles; whether a job slows a concurrent re-encode below real time (real processes); what the worker image gains in size. Any task that follows must carry: the track is labelled machine-made wherever it is listed; invented captions stay under a bound the spike measured; it is opt-in per library and the default image and install are unchanged; it never slows a viewer's re-encode below real time; languages it serves badly are written down as a gap; it runs only on the operator's servers (D-037). Translation of an existing track waits on the same count.

items.title: A subtitle file beside the film that is out of sync stays out of sync
items.notes: AI research 2026-11-20 (D-036). Not a model: speech detection and alignment, about 20-30 s per film (the tool's own figure, unverified here), stored as an offset applied on delivery with no file touched. Promote on data: the share of dogfood sidecar text subtitles whose estimated offset is over 0.5 s, or a viewer issue with a capture. Needs JS-095's queue. A film with cuts cannot be fixed by one offset, and that would be a written gap.

items.title: A client that turns on an image subtitle by default starts a whole-film read on the first play of each such film
items.notes: Dogfood report 2026-11-20 (D-038): one sighting, 46.7 GB read for one film when Moonfin's default subtitle mode chose an image track. D-003 accepts the read; JS-141 and JS-143 cover it. Promote JS-141 ahead of JS-135 if JS-143's count shows more than a few such reads a week, or most of those plays abandoned early. JS-154: job 82 ran at 0.6x beside this extraction on the same 4 cores, against 0.85x alone; the dogfood's log shows the extraction starting beside jobs 82 and 85, and job 83 within its run. JS-161's design review decides whether an extraction counts against capacity (D-044).

items.notes: Dogfood report 2026-11-20 (D-038): index 4 (a Chinese PGS track) where its rules pick English index 3; index 5 (the second English track) where index 4 exists. Possibly the index numbering of main's item, which hides non-default audio tracks (JS-147 lists them). items.title: Where no transcode can run, the details item names the browser's track for every client, though a client that switches tracks itself could play the saved language
items.notes: D-029, D-034 (JS-147): in the lasting states (no transcodeStore, no probed duration, no live worker that runs transcodes, differing stores) the item names and lists the track a browser will hear; PlaybackInfo for a self-switching client still names and plays the saved-language track. Promote to a task ahead of other open work if JS-075 records a supported client starting from the item's track; drop if none does. The design-around to assess then is an item answer that depends on the client.

items.title: A viewer cannot take an abandoned film or show off Continue Watching or Next Up without losing its position
items.notes: Issue #233. An extension beyond Jellyfin; whether any supported app could show the control is unverified. Promote when the dogfood shows resume rows holding items with no progress for 30 days or more on several accounts, and a supported app (docs/status.md) can show the control; D-027: no work for one client alone.

items.title: A viewer who seeks mid-play into a part of a film that cannot be made sees a stopped picture and no reason (jellyfin-web)
items.notes: D-040, invariant 37. Probe, before any build: does any honest signal reach jellyfin-web's dialog or a message after playback has begun: a server-to-session message over the WebSocket jellyfin-web opens (/socket; whether jellyscale sends anything on it is unverified), or the offered duration or seek range ending where the file's readable part ends (invariant 40), so the seek cannot be made at all. 403 and 410 are expected to behave as 500 (the handler destroys the player on any answer of 400 or more) and need one observation at most. Promote when: the dogfood's log shows the once-per-job line for a file-caused segment failure after playback began at all (one occurrence schedules the probe; a repeat makes it a task ahead of new features), or a probe finds a working signal cheaply. Drop if: JS-075's native-client captures show they explain it themselves and the dogfood count stays at zero over a month of use.

items.title: A refused playback decision line does not say whether a copy or a re-encode was refused
items.notes: JS-153 minor. The refused line carries one refusal reason and no asked method, where a direct play that gave up a transcode carries asked and asked_reasons. WorkersAtCopyBound implies a copy; NoWorkerWithFreeCores, NoWorkerRunning and RememberedFailure do not say. An operator sizing workers cannot tell a cheap copy refused from a re-encode refused without looking up the film. Refusals on the dogfood: unverified. Promote as a criterion (the refused line and jellyscale_playbackinfo_refusals_total carry what was asked, with its reasons) when jellyscale_playbackinfo_refusals_total on the dogfood is above zero for a reason that does not name the method, or when JS-154's decision chooses refusing with a reason: the task that does it carries the criterion. D-041.

Whether a helper on the cores left beside a 0.8-core job keeps the first viewer at real time is unverified. items.notes: D-052 keeps helpers off the worker running the viewers' own job. Promote when a measurement shows a same-worker helper brings such a job to 1.0x or above, or when the dogfood (JS-166, the 12-thread node) shows a job under 1.2x on a worker with at least the job's cost free and no other worker to help.
